review.limitations: Not every parameterized rule or derivation was independently reconstructed; the article presents schematic architectural analyses.

evidence.description: Explicit changes to core composition and rule ordering
Worked houses, interpretive alternatives and constraints

sections.title: In brief
sections.text: The Part 2 framework is applied to Wright’s Prairie and L-shaped Usonian houses.

sections.title: Question
sections.text: Can their apparent formal differences be explained through explicit changes to a generative organization?

sections.title: Main claim
sections.text: Basic Usonian compositions can be interpreted as transformations of the Prairie grammar, while maintaining related rule dependencies.

sections.title: Method
sections.text: Rewrite a modified subset of Koning–Eizenberg’s Prairie grammar in normal form. Change the fireplace into an interior kitchen/fireplace workspace, rearrange zones and make extensions optional.

sections.title: Examples
sections.text: A Garrison-house derivation and plans for Jacobs, Lusk, Newman, Rosenbaum and Pope illustrate compositions elaborated with ornamentation rules.

sections.title: Conclusion
sections.text: A block-based interpretation connects the two languages explicitly. Knight argues that linked grammars can strengthen an analysis of style while allowing alternative interpretations.

sections.title: Limits
sections.text: The normal-form Prairie grammar omits some original rules and admits some additional possibilities. A formal connection is an interpretation, not proof that Wright followed this exact procedure.

sections.title: Why read it
sections.text: Changing control can matter as much as changing shape: obligatory versus optional extensions changes the organization of possible plans.

terms.meaning: A change applied to a selected subset of a grammar rather than every rule.
